lesson.text: Remember? Prefixes and suffixes help you work out a word. The words around it help too!
Context clues: the rest of the sentence can explain a new word. "The puppy was so exhausted after the long walk that it fell asleep at once." Exhausted must mean very tired.
Literal words mean exactly what they say: "The cat sat on the mat." Non-literal words mean something else: "It's raining cats and dogs" means it is raining very hard.
More non-literal phrases: "a piece of cake" means very easy. "Over the moon" means very happy. "Take steps" means do things to make something happen.
Some words mean nearly the same but differ in strength. "I knew" is sure. "I believed" is fairly sure. "I guessed" is not sure at all.
Feelings have shades too: glad, happy, delighted, overjoyed, each a little stronger. And ways to walk: stroll, walk, march, dash. Choose the word that fits exactly.
Try it in the world: describe your buddy three ways, from weaker to stronger: "My buddy is glad, happy, overjoyed!" Then find a non-literal phrase for your best build. Next: writing a story.

exercises.prompt: "It's raining cats and dogs." What does this mean?
exercises.explain: It is non-literal: it means heavy rain.

exercises.prompt: "The test was a piece of cake." What does this mean?
exercises.explain: A piece of cake means very easy.

exercises.prompt: Literal words mean exactly what they say.
exercises.hint: The cat sat on the mat.
exercises.explain: True: literal words say exactly what they mean.

exercises.prompt: "Zara was over the moon with her prize." How did she feel?
exercises.hint: Did she really jump over the Moon?
exercises.explain: Over the moon means very happy.

exercises.prompt: "The puppy was so exhausted after the long walk that it fell asleep at once." What does exhausted mean?
exercises.hint: What did the puppy do right away?
exercises.explain: Falling asleep at once is the clue: exhausted means very tired.

exercises.prompt: "The soup was scalding, so Bram waited for it to cool." What does scalding mean?
exercises.hint: He waited for it to cool.
exercises.explain: It needed to cool, so scalding means very hot.

exercises.hint: Which one means exactly what it says?
choices: He has a heart of gold.
exercises.explain: The dog really chased the ball.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order from least sure to most sure.
exercises.hint: Which word shows you are certain?
exercises.explain: Guessed is not sure, believed is fairly sure, knew is sure.

exercises.prompt: "Nell took steps to keep her garden safe." What does took steps mean?
choices: did things to make it happen
exercises.explain: Take steps is non-literal: she did things to protect her garden.

exercises.prompt: "The desert was arid; no rain had fallen for months." What does arid mean?
exercises.hint: What does no rain for months tell you?
exercises.explain: No rain for months means the desert was very dry: arid.

exercises.prompt: Put these in order from the weakest feeling to the strongest.
exercises.hint: Which word is the biggest happy?
exercises.explain: glad, happy, delighted, overjoyed: each is a bit stronger.

exercises.prompt: Which word fits best? "The runner ___ to the finish line."
exercises.explain: Dashed means ran very fast; strolled and wandered are slow.

exercises.prompt: "I ___ it would rain, but I was not sure." Which word fits?
exercises.explain: Guessed shows you are not sure; knew would mean sure.

exercises.prompt: "Break a leg!" means you should hurt yourself.
exercises.hint: It is said to actors before a show.
exercises.explain: False: it is non-literal. It means good luck!

exercises.prompt: "The tiny mouse peered out of the hole, then darted away." What does darted mean?
exercises.hint: How does a scared mouse move?
exercises.explain: A mouse darting away moves very quickly.

exercises.prompt: Match each phrase to its meaning.
exercises.hint: These are non-literal: what do they really mean?
exercises.explain: A piece of cake is very easy, over the moon is very happy, and raining cats and dogs is heavy rain.

exercises.prompt: Sort the sentences: literal or non-literal?
items: The cat sat on the mat.
I ate a piece of cake at tea.
The test was a piece of cake.
exercises.hint: Does it mean exactly what the words say?
exercises.explain: A cat on a mat and cake at tea are literal. Raining cats and dogs, and a test that was a piece of cake, mean something else.

exercises.prompt: Order the ways of moving, from the slowest to the fastest.
exercises.hint: Which one is a slow, relaxed walk? Which one is a sudden run?
exercises.explain: Stroll is slow and relaxed, walk is ordinary, march is quick and firm, and dash is a sudden run.

exercises.prompt: Use the clues around each word. Match ravenous, gloomy, timid and soaked to their meanings.
items: a ravenous fox ate it all
a gloomy cave, hard to see in
exercises.hint: Look at what happens next in each phrase: eating it all, hard to see, hiding, puddles.
exercises.explain: The fox ate it all, so ravenous means very hungry. It was hard to see, so gloomy means dark. The mouse hid, so timid means shy. Puddles show soaked means very wet.
